analysis.one_liner: Requires for-profit and private equity owners of hospitals and clinics to disclose finances, get licenses, and fund closure protections.
analysis.headline: Introduced July 23, 2026 by Senator Markey with seven Democratic and independent cosponsors, and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled since.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make for-profit corporations that own hospitals, doctor practices, nursing homes, hospices, and other health care providers publicly report their finances, including debt, fees, executive pay, staffing levels, wage cuts, and closures. Private equity funds would need a federal license to buy health care companies, revocable for price gouging or understaffing, and regulators could freeze new purchases while a task force studies the problem. Hospitals would have to give 90 days notice before closing or cutting essential services, and pension debts owed to workers would move to the front of the line in health care bankruptcies.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients in communities served by private equity-owned or for-profit hospitals, nursing homes, and hospices, who would learn who owns their providers and how they are financed. Health workers gain required reporting of staffing ratios, wage cuts, and labor law complaints, and pension obligations would be paid first if a health care company goes bankrupt. Communities facing a hospital closure would get 90 days notice, a public comment period, and a plan to preserve access to essential services.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients, health workers, and communities facing closures

how_it_helps.text: For-profit owners of health care entities must publicly report ten years of financial data: debt levels, fees collected by private equity owners, executive salaries, dividends extracted, staffing levels and staff-to-patient ratios, wage and benefit reductions, facility closures, and worker protection complaints.

Private equity funds must obtain a license from the Secretary of Health and Human Services to invest in or purchase a health care entity; the license can be denied or revoked for price gouging, understaffing, or access barriers, and revocation forces divestment.

The Secretary may prohibit private equity funds from purchasing health care companies until a new task force has studied whether abuses such as understaffing and access barriers are occurring in specific health care sectors.

Hospitals must notify the Secretary at least 90 days before discontinuing essential services or closing, submit a mitigation plan to preserve access, and submit to a public comment period of at least 45 days; hospitals that violate the rules can be barred from Medicare enrollment for up to three years.

In health care bankruptcies, pension withdrawal liability owed under ERISA would be paid before other claims, and bankruptcy courts would have to give substantial weight to regional health care access when approving a health care company's reorganization plan.

Health care companies and private equity funds must report all political spending, including lobbying and contributions to groups that do not disclose donors, and health care real estate investment trusts would lose favorable tax treatment on rents from health care property.

analysis.who_pays: Private equity funds, health care real estate investment trusts, and for-profit health care corporations. They would bear license fees, potential five-year escrow requirements covering operating costs, civil fines, the cost of ten years of financial disclosure, and the loss of REIT tax treatment on health care rents.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private equity funds, REITs, and for-profit health care companies

drawbacks.text: The disclosure demands are extensive: each covered firm must report roughly three dozen categories of information for each of the previous ten years, and even the bill directs the Secretary to reduce the administrative burden, which suggests drafters recognized the compliance cost is heavy and could be passed on in prices.

License requirements, possible five-year escrow accounts covering operating and capital costs, and an acquisition freeze could deter capital from flowing into struggling rural or safety-net facilities that need outside investment to survive, potentially hastening the closures the bill aims to prevent.

Key standards are open-ended: the Secretary decides what counts as 'price gauging,' services that would 'place the public health at risk,' and whether a sale-leaseback would 'weaken financial status,' giving one department wide discretion over acquisitions and hospital finances.
The general civil penalty for violating the new title is capped at $10,000 per violation, which may be small relative to the finances of the firms being regulated.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core transparency provisions are low-risk: telling the public who owns their hospital and how it is financed imposes costs mainly on the owners. The stronger tools carry real tradeoffs. A licensing regime and acquisition freeze give the executive branch broad discretion over who may own health care, and heavy escrow and disclosure requirements could push capital away from exactly the fragile facilities the bill wants to protect. The hospital closure notice and mitigation process, and the bankruptcy rule putting worker pensions first, are the provisions with the clearest and most direct public benefit; the compliance burden and vagueness of the enforcement standards are the honest costs an supporter would have to acknowledge.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, and no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled since.

narrative.text: Senator Markey introduced the bill on July 23, 2026, joined by seven cosponsors: Senator Sanders (Independent) and six Democrats.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day.
The action history lists no further steps: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No final winner exists yet. As of now, the private equity funds, real estate trusts, and for-profit health care companies the bill would regulate continue operating under current rules while the bill sits without committee action, and the communities and workers the bill would protect have gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: So far, private equity and health care REITs

sides.party_line_note: All eight sponsors are Democrats plus one Independent; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-chaired Finance Committee has taken no action since referral.

industries.note: The bill requires a federal license to buy health care companies, allows the government to freeze acquisitions while a task force studies abuses, mandates disclosure of fees, debt, and extracted dividends, and can force divestment for understaffing or price gouging. Studies cited in the bill's design treat private equity cost-cutting in hospitals and nursing homes as a patient safety problem, so the industry's interest in unrestricted buying runs against patient access.

industries.industry: Health care real estate investment trusts (REITs)
industries.note: The bill bars sale-leaseback deals whose terms would weaken a hospital's finances or risk public health, and rewrites the tax code so rents from health care property no longer qualify for REIT-favorable treatment. Sale-leasebacks are a common way owners pull cash out of hospital buildings, leaving the operating hospital with the rent bill.

industries.industry: For-profit hospital, nursing home, and hospice chains
industries.note: These companies face ten years of financial disclosure, staffing and wage-cut reporting, closure notice and mitigation requirements, and potential Medicare enrollment bans for violations. Firms without private equity owners face a lighter disclosure list, and transparent ownership data could help well-run operators distinguish themselves.

industries.industry: Registered investment companies (mutual funds and similar funds)
industries.note: The bill makes it unlawful for any registered investment company to strip an asset from a health care entity or otherwise undermine care quality or access, with the SEC writing rules in consultation with HHS. Most such funds hold health care stocks without controlling them, so the practical burden is likely small but the prohibition is broad.

analysis.trajectory: The bill is in a Republican-chaired committee with no Republican support and no action since its July 2026 referral. With the Congress ending January 3, 2027, the realistic path is that it sits without a hearing or vote, as most health care bills referred to Senate Finance do, unless its sponsors attach provisions to a larger moving bill.
